chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
title: Putney Dandridge recording dates and getting paid
summary: McRae explains that studio dates were one-off jobs, paid at the union, whose records were sometimes released in Europe first.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: stages of you joining Chick Webb, there's some recordings that you made also with -- You made a Red Allen recording, you made the Putney Dandridge recordings.
Yeah.
How about Putney Dandridge? You had a solo on a couple of those, I believe. Was he a well known vocalist at that time?
Yeah, he was. Pretty well, yeah. That's right.
Tell us some things about it.
You see, this is another gig.
I know these are all --
These are recording dates. These are dates that you set up. It's the same thing sometime that how you can make a recording -- and I forget.
Do you know the label that was made on?
Vocalion.

Independent at that time, right.
Now you see, you would make these dates -- you make these dates with these different combos and different set-ups and things like that, you know.
And you probably wouldn't even hear them.
Because you just go into the studio and record them --
Go into the studio and you make a recording, go to the union and pick up your money.
And these companies sometime wouldn't release them for maybe another year. They would probably release them in Europe first.
Then they would release them over here. Sometime you would forget about you even made
